notes.meaning: Faith gives a real and present certainty to the good things God has promised for the future. It acts like an inner sight that proves the reality of what our physical eyes cannot see. By trusting God's bare word, a believer treats His promises as already true and solid.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some Word of Faith teachers explain faith here as a literal, tangible force that believers can use to bring things into reality, rather than personal trust in God's promises.

notes.meaning: God gave His warm approval to the faithful people who lived in Old Testament times. Their firm trust in God was the true reason Scripture honors them and holds them up as examples. Their lives proved that genuine faith, and not mere human effort, is what pleases the Lord.

We understand through faith that God created the entire universe simply by speaking His command. He did not build the world out of existing materials that were already visible, but called everything into being out of nothing. Our minds grasp this vast work because we accept God's own record in Scripture as true.

Abel offered an animal sacrifice in faith, showing he knew he needed an atonement—a covering for sin through shed blood. God openly showed approval of Abel and his gifts, likely by sending down fire to consume the sacrifice. Even though Abel died long ago, his story still speaks to us about coming to God through faith.

Enoch walked closely with God in faith and was taken straight to heaven without having to die. Before God took him, Scripture testified that his holy life pleased the Lord. His miraculous departure showed the ancient world that a real life with God exists beyond the grave.

No one can please God without faith, because coming to Him in prayer or worship requires trust. Anyone who approaches God must believe that He truly exists and that He actively rewards those who sincerely seek Him. Without this confidence in God's goodness, our religious acts have no real life.

Noah trusted God when he was warned about a great flood that had never been seen before. Moved by holy respect, he spent many long years building an ark to keep his family safe. By his obedience, he condemned the unbelieving world and became an heir of righteousness, which means being counted right with God through faith.

When God called Abraham to leave his homeland for a place he would receive later, he obeyed right away. He set out on a dangerous journey even though he did not know where he was going. His complete willingness to follow showed how firmly he trusted God to guide him.

Even after reaching the promised land, Abraham lived in tents as a foreigner rather than taking permanent ownership of the country. Isaac and Jacob shared this same unsettled lifestyle with him as fellow heirs of God's promise. Their movable tents showed they were patiently waiting for what God would give them later.

Abraham was content to live in tents because he was looking forward to an everlasting city with permanent foundations. This heavenly city is designed, built, and finished by God Himself. Abraham knew that earth could never provide a lasting home for an immortal soul.

Sarah was enabled to conceive a child even though she had always been barren and was far past the normal age for motherhood. Although she doubted and laughed at first, she came to trust that God was completely faithful to keep His word. Her faith rested on God's power when natural circumstances offered no hope at all.

Because of this faith, an enormous family came from one elderly man whose body was as good as dead for fathering children. Abraham's descendants grew to be as countless as the stars in the night sky and the grains of sand on the seashore. God showed that His supernatural power can bring a whole nation out of human helplessness.

These patriarchs died while still holding firmly to their faith, even though they had not yet received the full blessings God had promised. They saw those promises from far away, welcomed them joyfully, and openly admitted that they were only travelers passing through the earth. Faith made future blessings so real to them that they rested in them even at the hour of death.

When believers speak of themselves as travelers, they make it clear that they are searching for a homeland of their own. If Abraham and his family had been yearning for the country they left behind, they had plenty of time and opportunity to go back. Instead, they freely chose to stay on their journey with God.

The patriarchs were longing for a much better home, a heavenly country prepared by God. Because they trusted Him and lived for that eternal home, God was not ashamed to be known as their God. In fact, He prepared a glorious city for them to live in forever.

When God tested Abraham, he was ready to offer his beloved son Isaac on the altar as a sacrifice. This was an astonishing test because God had specifically promised that Abraham's descendants and the Savior would come through Isaac. Giving up his only child of promise meant trusting God above his deepest natural feelings and human logic.

Abraham reasoned that God was powerful enough to raise Isaac back from the dead to keep His promise. In a figurative sense, Abraham did receive his son back from death, since he had already fully surrendered him to die. This event served as a picture of how God would later offer His own Son and raise Him to life.

By faith, Isaac spoke prophetic blessings over his two sons, Jacob and Esau, regarding what would happen in their future. Even though he had initially favored Esau, Isaac submitted to God's purpose by giving the primary spiritual blessing to the younger son, Jacob. He trusted completely that God would bring these future events to pass.

When Jacob was near death, he gave God's blessing to both of Joseph's sons and knowingly placed the chief blessing on the younger son. As he finished his instructions, he bowed in worship while leaning on the top of his staff. His staff showed his physical weakness as an old man and his lifelong posture as a pilgrim waiting on God.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: An older Latin reading translated this phrase as Jacob adoring the top of Joseph's staff, which traditional Catholic commentators explained as honoring the ruler's staff as a figure of authority or Christ.

notes.meaning: Facing his own death in Egypt, Joseph spoke with certainty about the future departure of Israel to the promised land. He gave strict orders that his bones should not remain in Egypt, but be carried with the people when God led them out. His unburied coffin served as a lasting witness to Israel that God would surely fulfill His ancient promise.

When Moses was born, his parents hid him for three months because they saw something special and God-given in his appearance. They were not terrified by Pharaoh's wicked order to drown every baby boy. Their trust in God gave them courage to risk their own lives to protect their child.

When Moses reached adulthood, he deliberately gave up the royal rank of being the son of Pharaoh's daughter. He chose instead to share the harsh suffering of God's enslaved people rather than enjoy the short-lived pleasures of the Egyptian court. Faith helped him see that worldly pleasure quickly fades, while God's favor lasts forever.

Moses considered the disgrace of suffering for the promised Messiah to be of greater value than all the wealth of Egypt. He made this choice because he kept his eyes fixed on the eternal reward God gives to the faithful. He knew that any shame borne for God would end in everlasting glory.

Moses marched out of Egypt without being paralyzed by the furious anger of Pharaoh. He stood firm through every trial because his faith enabled him to see the invisible God walking with him. Looking to God gave him courage that outmatched any human threat.

Moses obeyed God by establishing the Passover meal and ordering the blood of the lamb to be sprinkled on the doorposts. This blood protected the Israelite families so that the angel of death would pass over them without killing their oldest sons. It pointed ahead to how sinners are saved from God's wrath through the shed blood of Christ.

The people of Israel walked straight through the Red Sea on dry ground because they trusted God's command. When the Egyptian army tried to cross the same sea by their own strength, the waters rushed back and drowned them all. What was safe passage for the believer became sudden destruction for the presumptuous unbeliever.

The fortified walls of Jericho crashed down after the army of Israel obediently marched around them once a day for seven days. Marching and blowing ram horns could not bring down stone walls by natural means, but God did it in response to their faith. Their steady obedience proved that God's power wins the victory when His people trust His word.

Rahab the prostitute was not destroyed along with the rebellious people of Jericho because she welcomed Israel's spies in peace. Even though she had lived a sinful life and belonged to a pagan nation, she believed that the God of Israel was the true God of heaven and earth. Her faith led to repentance and brought her safely into the family of God's people.

The writer explains that there is not enough time to tell the full stories of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets. Each of these men faced huge challenges and had personal flaws, yet God used them mightily when they put their trust in Him. Their lives show that true faith can operate in all kinds of people and situations.

Through faith, God's servants conquered hostile kingdoms, ruled justly, received what God promised, and shut the mouths of ravenous lions. Others survived scorching furnace fires and escaped being killed by swords, while the weak were given supernatural strength to win battles and rout foreign armies. These great victories showed that God's power rescues and strengthens those who depend on Him.

In some cases, grieving mothers received their dead children raised back to life through the faith of the prophets. Yet other faithful people were brutally tortured and refused to buy their freedom by giving up their faith, because they were looking forward to a far better resurrection. Faith does not always lead to an earthly rescue; it also gives the courage to die well for God.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching points to this passage as an explicit reference to the martyrdom of the mother and her seven sons in 2 Maccabees 7, which supports the authority of the deuterocanonical books as Scripture.

notes.meaning: Many other believers were put to the test by cruel mocking, whipping, heavy chains, and harsh imprisonment. They were treated like criminals simply because they stayed loyal to God. Faith supported their spirits even when they were stripped of all freedom and dignity.

Some of God's witnesses were stoned to death, sawed in half, tempted to renounce God, or killed by the sword. Others survived only as homeless refugees clothed in rough sheepskins and goatskins, hiding in deserts, mountains, and caves. The world treated them as outcasts, but God declared that the world was not worthy of having such holy men and women in it.

All these Old Testament saints received God's high praise for their steadfast faith, yet they died without receiving the ultimate promise in their lifetime. God waited so He could provide something far better for us under the gospel, which is the full work of Jesus Christ. His plan was that Old Testament believers and New Testament Christians would reach final perfection together in glory.
